metadata.title: Walker Tower Defense: Inside the Godot Code
metadata.audience: makers following the channel's Claude + Walker game workflows
metadata.note: godot-gamedev walker film. Code panels are Godot editor reconstructions with verbatim source; each is followed by real engine output of the same build. No game change, no paid calls, no upload.

beats.narration_text: Merhaba — this is Liam, in for Bear. That's the kind of prompt Walker expects, reconstructed here, not a transcript. This time we open the project itself: a piece of code, then the exact thing it does on screen, in the real build.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a four-element tower defense — Fire, Ice, Poison and Storm towers on a 12-by-8 grid, where every tower you build reshapes the monsters' route — into a playable Godot project.
props.runningText: illustrative reconstruction — not the historical prompt
output: Built: one 6-line scene file and about 3,000 lines of GDScript.
Every visual drawn in code; 65 automated checks.

beats.narration_text: Walker Tower Defense is built from script and draw calls. It's one six-line scene, about three thousand lines of GDScript, and not a single image file. So every piece of code we read has a result you can watch.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant writer: text is typed on screen over the narration, so mid-beat samples legitimately show a partial page. The finished text fills the safe area and holds for the last 1.5 s.

beats.narration_text: Open the scene file and there's one node. Run it, and the session script builds the rest: the board, a canvas layer for the HUD, one node per tower and monster. Not one of them is named — the live tree reads at-Node2D-at-two. The tidy Grid and Hud in the project's own brief are descriptions, not node names.

beats.narration_text: Here's the entire scene file. One Node2D, one script attached: session dot g d. There's no Grid node to click on in the editor, no HUD scene, no tower prefab. Everything is built in code when the game starts, which keeps the whole project as diffable text.

beats.narration_text: Input is registered in code too. Setup-input adds every action — confirm, pause, restart, next wave, the number keys — to Godot's InputMap at startup. This function once vanished in a rewrite. Fifty-six tests stayed green, because none of them pressed a key, and the whole keyboard was dead.

beats.narration_text: This is the rule the Unity original didn't have. The level's JSON and a tile-kind table decide what's walkable. Before a tower is placed, the grid pretends it's already there, then runs A-star from the spawn, and from every monster's current cell, to the exit. Any failure, and the placement is refused.

props.title: The Rule the Original Lacked
props.source: godot/features/grid/grid.gd:152-162 at caf082c · Godot editor reconstruction

notes.label: Unity source
notes.value: no route check; stranded monsters teleported

cues.label: the new cell counts as blocked

beats.narration_text: Here it is refusing: a tower beside the spawn is fine; the one that would seal the corner is not — would block the path. Then a tower dropped onto the road passes the same check, and the route tint bends round it.

beats.narration_text: The pacing fix is two constants. The Unity timings assumed a tile was one unit; this board draws a tile at sixty-four pixels, and monsters crawled at forty-four pixels a second. Instead of rewriting every recovered number, the whole simulation clock runs three times faster, and the player can multiply that by one, two or three.

props.title: The Pacing Fix Is a Clock
props.source: godot/game/session.gd:21-30 at caf082c · Godot editor reconstruction
props.code:
## The Unity values were authored for a board where one tile was roughly one
## Unity unit. This board draws a tile at 64 px, so the same durations read as
## a crawl -- monsters crossed at 44 px/sec and wave 1 took 26 seconds.
##
## Rather than rewrite the recovered numbers (which would destroy the fidelity
## checks in tests/test_data.gd), the whole simulation clock runs faster.
## Every duration and speed scales together, so the recovered RATIOS are
## untouched: a tower still deals exactly the same damage per monster pass.
const BASE_SIM_SPEED := 3.0
const SPEED_STEPS: Array[int] = [1, 2, 3]

cues.label: a tile was one Unity unit

beats.narration_text: Watch the speed readout: the button takes it to two, F to three, and back to one. The rules don't change, only the clock — every duration scales together, so a tower still lands the same damage per pass.

beats.narration_text: Every hit in the game lands here. One number in, subtracted from health: no element, no resistance, no colour check. That's why the elemental tower defense has no elemental damage. Hit-flash is set first, a brief wash toward white. The health it subtracts from comes from the wave spawner's compounding ramp.

props.title: Every Hit Lands Here

notes.label: hit_flash
notes.value: 0.14 s white wash, added in b67653a

beats.narration_text: Each hit lands in that function: a white flash, a shorter bar, and at zero, four gold.

beats.narration_text: Poison runs through the same door. Every tenth of a second of simulated time, a poison tick calls take-damage, and take-damage resets hit-flash. The flash never gets the chance to fade. So the green poison tint, drawn first, is washed toward white for as long as the poison lasts.

props.title: Poison Goes Through the Same Door
props.source: godot/features/monsters/monster.gd:74-84 at caf082c · Godot editor reconstruction

beats.narration_text: And there it is in wave two: the poisoned monster at the front stays pale the whole time. Two systems, each reasonable alone, combine into a status a player may not read as poison.

beats.narration_text: Storm's chain picks the nearest live monster within reach of its current target, and flips a coin on whether to skip the one it just hit, so a chain can bounce back and forth. That quirk is from the Unity source, kept on purpose. The beam's lifetimes, four-tenths and two-tenths of a second, run on the three-times clock.

props.title: How Storm Chooses a Neighbour

notes.label: Coin flip
notes.value: may re-pick the previous target (Unity quirk, kept)

notes.label: Beam life
notes.value: 0.4 s then 0.2 s per hop, on the 3x clock

beats.narration_text: Real speed first: the beam hits, hops to the neighbour, and it's gone — six frames. Again at an eighth of the speed. The code does exactly what it says; whether a person sees a chain is a different question.

beats.narration_text: The F1 overlay is drawn by the session itself, in its own draw function, at x eight to three thirty-eight. But the grid is a child of the session, added in ready, starting at x ninety-six — and in Godot, children draw after their parent. So the board is painted straight over most of the overlay.

beats.narration_text: All the art is code. This is the end of draw-tower-body: Storm's bolt is a six-point polygon, and the upgrade marker is a three-point chevron in the same yellow — shape, not just colour. The same function draws the placed tower, the build-bar miniature and the placement ghost, and the stats behind them live in one tuning table.

props.title: All the Art Is Code

TowerTuning.Element.STORM:
			canvas.draw_colored_polygon(PackedVector2Array([
				Vector2(2, -36), Vector2(-6, -25), Vector2(-1, -25),

beats.narration_text: Tests get their own look. This is the keyboard suite's core: it builds real key events and pushes them through Input dot parse-input-event, so they travel the path a player's do. That's the difference from the other suites, which call session methods directly: fast, deterministic, and blind to input.

props.title: A Test That Presses Keys
props.source: godot/tests/test_keyboard.gd:33-41 at caf082c · Godot editor reconstruction

beats.narration_text: These are the recorded receipts, not a demo. With the one-line fix reverted, eight of nine keyboard checks fail; with it restored, nine of nine pass. What a passing suite still can't tell you is whether a refusal can be read in three-tenths of a second, or whether poison looks like poison. That takes footage, and a person.

props.title: Recorded Keyboard-Suite Receipts
props.note: Recorded receipts, 2026-09-21 and 2026-09-28. Synthetic key events, not play.

beats.narration_text: One more comment worth testing. If the level file fails to load, this branch keeps the state at menu, and the comment promises the session stays out of playing. But nothing stops Enter from starting a session later, and the menu-card HUD is drawn on a canvas layer above the error panel.

props.title: A Comment Nobody Tested
props.source: godot/game/session.gd:91-96 at caf082c · Godot editor reconstruction
props.code:
grid = Grid.new()
	add_child(grid)
	if not grid.load_level("res://levels/level_01.json"):
		# Board could not be built. _draw shows the reason instead of a
		# half-initialised grid, and the session stays out of PLAYING.
		state = State.MENU

notes.label: HUD
notes.value: CanvasLayer — drawn above the error panel

beats.narration_text: Staged, in a copy with the level's exit removed: the error panel sits under the menu card. Enter sets playing, Space even starts wave one, but the HUD never redraws. The comment was a promise nothing checked.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. This is a project you can read top to bottom as text, and its best habit, the input-only keyboard test, exists because of a real failure. The three defects I found are all draw order and layering: places where the code is right and the screen isn't. And a person still has to play it.

artifactLines: Implemented: one 6-line scene, ~3,000 lines of GDScript, every pixel from _draw().
Good habits: one fixed-step loop, recovered constants locked by tests, an input-only keyboard suite.
Defects on screen: F1 overlay under the board; error panel under the menu card; poison reads white.
Not judged here: fun, fairness, balance. That is a human playtest — 0 of 22 done.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude in your own Godot project: Use Walker on my Godot project. Pick one draw-order or layering assumption — which node or canvas layer paints over which — and predict what the player will see. Then write a capture that proves or disproves it with real input, and only after that, propose the smallest code change. Make the prediction before you look; it's the only way to find out whether you understand your own scene tree. Liam, in for Bear.
